evidence.text: A bird flying toward the sky 一
Pictograph of sepals of a flower. The meaning "no" is a phonetic loan.
鳥飛上翔不下來也。从一，一猶天也。象形。凡不之屬皆从不。

Pictogram (象形): the calyx of a flower. 不 was then composed into a phono-semantic character with the pictograph for mouth (口), to form 否 (OC *brɯʔ, *pɯʔ), representing “no” (negation). This composed meaning then spread back to the original character 不, making it a synonym of 否. A new character of 柎 (OC *po) was eventually created to represent the original meaning of calyx.
Following Shuowen’s interpretation, Karlgren and Wieger interpret it as a bird flying toward the sky (一). The sky being the limit for the bird, thus the idea of negation.
Old Chinese had two sets of negatives: the initial *p-series and the initial *m-series. 不 is the prototype of the *p-series of negatives. Although it is the usual Literary Chinese negative attested from the oracle bone script down, its current usage is now confined to Mandarin dialects. In the oracle bone inscriptions, a total of five negative particles can be found: 不, 弗, 毋, 勿 and 非. With the exception of 非 (discussed later), the remaining can be neatly organised into the following system:
Takashima (1996) argued that the *m-type negatives are modal (i.e. negative verbs which are thought of as controllable by the Shang), whereas the *p-type negatives are non-modal (imply uncontrollability; actions which are beyond the control of living persons).
In the *p-series, 不 usually goes with intransitive verbs in the oracle bone script, and 弗 (OC *pɯd) with transitive ones, although there are some glaring exceptions. Little or no pattern can be discerned in the *m-type category. Takashima (1996) also proposed that the difference between the two vowel series was whether they preceded “stative, eventive, passive” (*-V series) or “non-stative, non-eventive, active” (*-ɯd series) verbs.
It is possible that the two parallel series of negatives in Old Chinese represent a fusion of the common Sino–Tibetan *ma (“no, not”) (carried by the eastward-migrating early Sino–Tibetans) and an indigenous negation system in Central China, and that the merger had been complete by the Shang times. Compare a similar system in Proto-Tai: *ɓawᴮ (“not [strong form 1]”), *boːᴮ (“not [strong form 2]”), *miːᴬ (“not [weak form]”); Thai บ่ (bɔ̀ɔ, “(literary, archaic, dialectal) not”).
The development from Old Chinese to Middle Chinese was not regular. The character 不 replaced 弗 (OC *pɯd, MC *piut), to respect the naming taboo for Emperor Zhao of Han, although the pronunciation has remained in nearly all topolects (e.g. Beijing Mandarin bù, Guangzhou Cantonese bat¹, Meixian Hakka bud⁵, Shanghainese Wu peq). The Modern Standard Mandarin pronunciation is also from this checked coda word, but this word escaped from regular sound changes during its evolution to the modern pronunciation bù. The expected reading is fu (tone undetermined), with labiodentalisation. The rising-tone pronunciation had a Middle Chinese homophone 否 (“not”), which is now primarily used in compounds, and demonstrates the regular development into modern f-. Another example of a high-frequency word escaping this sound change is 父 (OC *paʔ, *baʔ, “dad”), which resulted in the late coinage of the character 爸 (bà).
不 is cognate with other negation particles in the *p-type category:
* 弗 (OC *pɯd, “not”);
* 非 (OC *pɯj, “not be; not”) – can be safely regarded as a fusion of 不 (OC *pɯ, *pɯʔ, *pɯ', “not”) and 惟 (OC *ɢʷi, “to be”);
* 否 (OC *brɯʔ, *pɯʔ, “not; to be wrong”);
* 匪 (OC *pɯjʔ, “it is not; to be not”); and
* 棐 (OC *pɯjʔ, “it is not; to be not”).
Cognate with Thai บ่ (bɔ̀ɔ, “(literary, archaic, dialectal) not”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Onomatopoeic.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解 / 甲骨金文字形、用法
evidence.text: The database reports two competing analyses of the oracle-bone and bronze graph: a ground line with root-like strokes, interpreted by some scholars as a plant root and linked by Chen Shihui to 茇; or a flower receptacle/calyx, identified by other scholars as the original graph for 柎. It also records 不 as a negative adverb in oracle-bone inscriptions, with an example glossed as a question about whether it will rain, and gives bronze-inscription uses for negation, ‘great’ (read 丕), a state name (邳), and personal or clan names. These are source-reported analyses and examples, not a settled derivation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：不

evidence.text: The database labels 不 the original form of 胚 and interprets the horizontal stroke as ground and the lower strokes as roots of a germinating seed. It separately notes the flower-calyx interpretation and says the graph was later borrowed for negation, leaving the original sense lost. The page lists oracle, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen stages, but its text does not give dated attestations for each stage.
evidence.title: 漢字「不」：字形演變

evidence.text: The article reviews the bird account in Shuowen and the flower-receptacle/calyx account advanced by earlier scholars, then questions whether the oracle-bone forms fit the flower interpretation. It also considers a root-related interpretation and concludes that the graph appears connected with plants or roots, while explicitly leaving its original sense unresolved for want of sufficient lexical evidence. The article records variant oracle and bronze forms and discusses forms whose lower strokes do not fit a calyx analysis.
evidence.title: 「不」字本義為花梢說質疑

evidence.source: Xu Shen, as quoted in the CUHK Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The quoted Shuowen explanation says 不 depicts a bird flying upward and not returning downward, with 一 representing the sky. This is a historical lexicographic explanation, not confirmation of the graph’s original referent; the modern database presents it alongside competing root and calyx analyses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：不

evidence.text: The authors place 不 as a general negative marker in oracle-bone inscriptions of the 14th–11th centuries BCE. They give an oracle-bone example 王不往于田, ‘the king will not go hunting,’ and note that scholarship has proposed several distinctions between 不 and other early negatives, including 弗; the distribution is debated. For later Archaic Chinese they identify 不 as a general verbal negative and cite examples from the Analects (dated in the article to 479–400 BCE) and Xunzi (4th century BCE). This documents the negative word’s uses, not the graphic origin of the sign.
evidence.title: A Typological Study of Negation in Sinitic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Views

evidence.field: Etymology / sound comparisons and modern readings
evidence.text: The page reports Old Chinese reconstructions for 不 as *pɯ, *pɯʔ, and *pɯ', and modern Standard Mandarin bù and Guangzhou Cantonese bat¹. It presents the calyx account and bird account as competing explanations, but its own references for the ancient forms are largely compiled through Richard Sears’s Chinese Etymology site. No historical sound value for the depicted plant or bird is independently established in the inspected sources, so these proposals do not support a demonstrated sound-loan match. The phonological reconstructions are not direct attestations of an object-name.
evidence.title: 不 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The page supplies no defensible decomposition into an independent semantic component plus a phonetic component. The database’s listed historical stages concern the graph 不 itself; the separate root and calyx proposals interpret the entire graph. The horizontal stroke and lower strokes are parts of those proposed depictions, not established sound components. There is therefore no supported component-to-character pronunciation comparison for a phonetic component.

evidence.text: The database describes the lower strokes as root-like strokes beneath a ground line and labels 不 the original form of 胚; it also notes an alternative calyx interpretation and a later borrowing for negation. These are reported analyses; the database does not establish an independent semantic-plus-phonetic component structure.

evidence.text: The database presents competing analyses: a horizontal ground line with root-like strokes, with Chen Shihui linking the graph to 茇, and a flower-calyx interpretation, with earlier scholars linking it to 柎. It quotes Shuowen’s bird-flying-upward account separately. Its entry reports oracle-bone use as a negative adverb, including 今至丁丑，其雨不？, and also as place, personal, and state names. editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

The sources do not independently establish the ancient pronunciation of any depicted object or an initial object-word/negative-word sound match.
